newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia cracks down on media to curb demo reports.
newsitem.headline: Serbia cracks down on media to curb demo reports.

text.p: Serbia closed an independent Belgrade radio station on Tuesday to halt its live reports of 16 days of opposition demonstrations aimed at ousting President Slobodan Milosevic.

Radio B-92 said the communications ministry ordered it to stop broadcasting while 50,000 students and opposition supporters took to the streets of Belgrade again in protest against election rigging by the ruling socialists.
Radio Index also disappeared from the air as the authorities cracked down on the independent media and state media accused the demonstrators of fomenting violence and "terrorism".
Staff at Radio Index could not immediately be reached but Radio B-92 said the ministry removed its frequency. The radio suffered frequent jamming during earlier demonstrations.
Five supreme court judges joined opposition to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and the United States warned Milosevic it would be "outraged" if he used police to crush the demonstrations.
The State Department called the local elections last month "a sham" after Milosevic denied the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties of victory in the capital and other cities.

The judges' revolt, in letters to the opposition daily Nasa Borba (Our Struggle), was the first sign of a crack in the machinery of state over which Milosevic has maintained a tight grip during nine years of authoritarian government.
Judge Zoran Ivosevic accused some of the 36 supreme court judges of being politically subservient and wrote:
"The Serbian supreme court has unfortunately not had the strength and the courage to give the electorate what belongs to it on the basis of the election results."
Serbian courts rubber-stamped socialist claims of unspecified "irregularities" in the elections to clear the way for fresh ballots which the socialists claimed they won.

A second protest letter, signed by Ivosevic and four judges belonging to the court, referred to the opposition claim of election robbery and said the legal profession should not be associated with theft.
The authorities, who have refrained from using police intervention so far, stepped up a media campaign against the opposition.
The opposition "wants to seize power by force" and its protests "concealed terrorism", wrote Vecernje Novosti, a mouthpiece for the socialist Party.
The harsh attacks were interpreted as a warning from Milosevic that he would not tolerate street protests indefinitely.
With no sign of the demonstrations flagging and international criticism growing, Milosevic was looking for a way out of the crisis to save face, diplomats said.
The government cancelled a parliament session for Tuesday when the Zajedno coalition had planned to stage its biggest protest yet to demand the alleged poll fraud be overturned.
Authorities, gambling the demonstrations would eventually fizzle out, cancelled the session to avoid possible clashes while the international spotlight was fixed on Belgrade.
The United States warned Milosevic that his refusal to recognise the result of the elections strengthened its resolve to keep the remaining U.N. sanctions against Belgrade.
These deny Serbia access to foreign credits it needs urgently to rebuild its economy.
Although anxious to get all sanctions removed, Milosevic has shown a willingness in the past to ignore international condemnation to maintain his grip on power.
